sections.heading: Living With Uveitis — Knowledge Base Overview
sections.intro:
This package synthesizes 29 sources from livingwithuveitis.com, a personal site written by one
uveitis patient (Wendy) over 2019–2024: eight educational reference pages covering uveitis basics,
eye anatomy, diagnostic tools, inflammation mechanism, and treatment options; eighteen first-person
blog posts documenting her own diagnosis, flares, procedures, and medication history in real time;
and three guest Q&A interviews with other uveitis patients she connected with through the site.

**This is a patient-voice corpus, not a clinical reference.** The reference pages cite published
research the author found and read herself, but the bulk of the material — the blog posts — is
lived experience: what a specific treatment felt like, what a doctor said in a specific
appointment, what worked for her and what didn't. Where a claim traces to cited research, the notes
preserve the citation; where it's personal experience, the notes preserve that too, and keep the
two visibly distinct rather than blending them into one authoritative voice. Two site pages
(`covid-19-uveitis`, `research-links`) were fetched but excluded from notes — see
`deferred_sources.txt` — because they are bare link lists with no first-person claims of their
own to cite.

subsections.body:
- **`01_CORE_PRINCIPLES.md`** — the recurring ideas across this collection: how uveitis is
  classified, why it resists the patient's own pattern-matching, and the treatment ladder from eye
  drops to biologics.
- **`07_PLAIN_ENGLISH_GLOSSARY.md`** — every technical term introduced across the collection,
  defined in plain English, alphabetical, no citations.
- **`09_SOURCE_CATALOG.md`** — auto-generated index of every source; do not hand-edit.
subsections.heading: What's in each file

subsections.body:
This collection is a single patient's account plus three guest interviews — it is not a
population-level epidemiological survey or a clinical practice guideline, even where it cites one.
Treatment details (dosing, side effects, procedure experience) reflect one person's course of
non-infectious posterior/panuveitis and multifocal choroiditis; a reader with a different uveitis
subtype (e.g. purely anterior, or infectious) would find less of this collection directly
applicable, though the classification and mechanism pages (`uveitis-overview`, `anatomy-of-the-eye`,
`inflammation`) are general.
subsections.heading: A note on scope

sections.heading: 01 — Core Principles
sections.intro:
The ideas below recur across the reference pages and the five years of blog posts in this
collection. They are not any single post's claim — they are the patterns visible once the
educational pages and the real-time patient narrative are read side by side.

---

subsections.body:
Uveitis is not one condition but a location-based (anterior, intermediate, posterior, panuveitis)
and duration-based (acute, recurrent, chronic) classification scheme, established by a 2004
specialist working group. Nearly every reference page and several blog posts hang their content on
this scaffold — see `uveitis-overview` and `anatomy-of-the-eye`. It also explains why two patients
with the "same" diagnosis can have very different disease: `qa-george`'s diagnosis
(Multifocal Choroiditis with panuveitis) and the site author's own (Multifocal Choroiditis,
described as posterior in `latest-on-my-uveitis`) share a name but differ in anatomic extent.
subsections.heading: The disease is classified along two independent axes: duration and location

subsections.body:
A pattern stated explicitly as early as `diagnosis-story` ("I never actually know how long
something's been going on in my eye before I see or feel symptoms") recurs across the entire
collection: a felt sense of stability is not evidence of disease control. `coping-when-treatment-fails` describes a flare that arrived with no warning during what felt like a stable period;
`prednisone-for-life`, the collection's most recent post, describes an identical pattern five years
later — "my eyes felt super good this morning... if not for the fundus photography... it likely
would have gone undetected." This is the direct rationale for the recurring imaging routine
described in `into-the-eyes-of-the-beholder` and `tools-tests-terms`: monitoring exists specifically
because the patient's own senses cannot be relied on.
subsections.heading: For posterior/chronic uveitis specifically, there is often no reliable subjective warning sign

subsections.body:
`treatment-complications` states this as an explicit thesis — "it's not the disease itself that
creates the most damage, but the complications and ancillary issues" — and the blog posts bear it
out repeatedly. Steroid treatment for inflammation causes cataracts and elevated eye pressure
(`prednisone-part-i`); pressure-lowering surgery for that steroid-induced pressure creates a bleb,
which can itself leak years later (`diffusing-the-bomb`); intravitreal injections repeated over
years require their own risk management (`intravitreal-injection-tutorial`). The chain of
complication-causing-complication is treated as the norm, not the exception.
subsections.heading: Complications more often come from treatment than from the disease directly

subsections.body:
`treatments-overview` frames the primary treatment decision as localized (drops, injections,
implants — affecting only the eye) versus systemic (oral or injected immunosuppression — affecting
the whole body), driven by whether the uveitis is tied to an identifiable systemic disease or is
idiopathic. The same tradeoff resurfaces in COVID-19-era clinical guidance summarized in
`prednisone-part-ii`, where expert consensus specifically favored local over systemic treatment
during active infection risk.
subsections.heading: Localized versus systemic treatment is the central treatment-ladder decision, not drug choice alone

subsections.body:
`coping-when-treatment-fails` cites a specific reframe — any single drug works roughly 50–70% of
the time, any approach 70–85%, nothing 100% — used to explain why a treatment that stops working
isn't evidence of a wrong diagnosis or a uniquely resistant case. This same graded view underlies
the collection's long medication-escalation arc (prednisone → antimetabolites → biologics →
localized injections) traced across `immunosuppressed-pnw`, `coping-when-treatment-fails`, and
`latest-on-my-uveitis`.
subsections.heading: Treatment "failure" is probabilistic and graded, not binary

subsections.body:
Three independent threads converge on this: standard risk categories and eligibility checklists
routinely fail to name uveitis specifically, forcing self-advocacy at the point of care
(`third-times-the-charm`, `new-year-same-blur`); an invisible disease in a young patient collides
with age-based assumptions about health (`qa-jack-pritchard`, `what-you-dont-see`); and low public
awareness of uveitis itself is named, independently, by three different patients as a primary
burden alongside the physical disease (`qa-george`, `qa-jack-pritchard`, `stories-support`).
subsections.heading: Being immunosuppressed for a rarely-recognized disease creates specific access and belief problems

subsections.body:
`treatments-overview` and `prednisone-part-i` both define a specific low-dose threshold (below
7.5mg) below which most prednisone side effects aren't typically experienced. `prednisone-for-life`
shows this playing out as a real clinical endpoint: after a year-long taper, the conclusion isn't
"keep reducing" but arriving at a specific, sustainable, low maintenance dose — going further
(to zero) triggered a subclinical recurrence.
subsections.heading: A steroid-sparing dose is a distinct, named treatment target — not simply "less than before"

subsections.body:
At least a third of uveitis cases have no identified cause (`uveitis-overview`). Where causes or
correlates are studied, the collection is careful to preserve the field's own uncertainty rather
than overstate it: `pregnancy-journey` cites competing hormonal and genetic explanations for why
women predominate among patients, and `race-and-disparity` explicitly states "correlation does not
equal causation" while surveying racial/ethnic differences in presentation and access to care.
subsections.heading: A substantial share of uveitis is idiopathic, and sex and race are documented but incompletely understood variables

sections.heading: Plain-English Glossary
sections.intro:
Terms introduced across this library's sources, defined in plain English. Alphabetical. No
citations here — see the individual source for the origin of each term.

**Adrenal crisis** — a rare, potentially fatal reaction to a lack of steroid hormone in the body,
most often a risk during abrupt steroid withdrawal after long-term use.

**Adrenocortical insufficiency** — the body's own cortisol production winding down because
supplemented steroid (like prednisone) has been telling the adrenal glands they aren't needed; the
reason stopping steroids abruptly is dangerous.

**Ahmed Glaucoma Valve** — a silicone drainage valve with a flow restrictor, implanted to reduce
eye pressure while preventing pressure from dropping too low right after surgery.

**Angiography (ocular)** — imaging the blood vessels in the eye using a fluorescent dye injected
into an arm vein; IVFA uses sodium fluorescein (yellow-green), ICG uses indocyanine green
(infrared, better for viewing the choroid).

**Anterior Chamber Flare** — cloudiness seen in the front of the eye when inflammation breaks down
the blood-aqueous barrier, letting cells and protein leak into the fluid there; a diagnostic sign
of uveitis.

**Antimetabolite** — a drug that interferes with a cell's normal metabolic processes, slowing the
immune system by blocking cell survival or multiplication (e.g. methotrexate, mycophenolate).

**Aqueous Shunt Implantation** — inserting a small tube to keep a drainage opening (created by a
trabeculectomy) from scarring shut.

**Auto-antibody** — an antibody that mistakenly targets and attacks the body's own tissues.

**Autoinflammatory disease** — disease driven by a genetic mutation in the innate immune system,
where the body reacts as though a pathogen is present even though none actually is — distinct from
autoimmune disease, which involves the adaptive immune system misidentifying self as foreign.

**Autologous blood injection** — a bleb-leak treatment where blood drawn from the patient's own arm
is injected into the leaking bleb to stimulate healing.

**Baerveldt / Molteno Glaucoma Implant** — pressure-reducing drainage implants without a built-in
valve; must be temporarily blocked with a stitch at surgery to prevent excessive early drainage.

**Bleb** — a small reservoir under the eye's surface, created by a trabeculectomy, that lets fluid
drain out of the eye in a controlled way. A **bleb leak** is a breach in this reservoir; risks
include infection (blebitis) and hypotony.

**Blebitis** — infection of a surgical bleb, an elevated risk for anyone with a history of
trabeculectomy.

**Blood-Retina Barrier (BRB)** — a two-layer barrier that selectively controls what can diffuse
into the retina, nourishing and protecting it.

**Calcineurin inhibitor** — a drug that blocks the enzyme calcineurin, which activates T-cells,
lowering immune activity (e.g. cyclosporine, tacrolimus).

**Choroid** — a network of blood vessels beneath the retina that supplies it with nutrients;
inflammation here is posterior uveitis (choroiditis).

**Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV)** — growth of new, abnormal, leaky blood vessels from the
choroid into the retina, a complication that can cause vision loss; when scarring follows, it's
called subretinal fibrosis.

**Ciliary body** — the eye structure connecting the iris to the choroid; controls lens shape for
focusing and is the part affected by intermediate uveitis.

**DEXA (Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry) Scan** — a scan measuring bone mineral density, used to
track bone loss risk from long-term steroid use.

**Dyschromatopsia** — deficient or inaccurate color vision.

**Exudate** — fluid, cells, and protein that leak out of blood vessels into nearby tissue.

**Granulomatous uveitis** — a form of anterior uveitis with a grainy appearance from clumped
keratic precipitates.

**HLA-B27 Gene** — a genetic marker strongly associated with autoimmune diseases including
anterior uveitis, though the underlying mechanism isn't established.

**Hypotony** — abnormally low eye pressure (below roughly 12 mmHg), which can distort the eye's
internal structure if it persists.

**Idiopathic** — no identifiable cause found; true for at least a third of uveitis cases.

**Immunomodulatory Treatment (IMT)** — treatment that works by activating or suppressing the
immune system; in uveitis, this generally means suppressing it.

**Intravitreal steroid implant injection** — injecting a slow-release corticosteroid implant
directly into the vitreous to treat inflammation locally rather than systemically.

**Iris** — the colored ring at the front of the eye that controls pupil size; the part affected by
anterior uveitis.

**Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)** — a childhood autoimmune arthritis that can cause uveitis
as an associated condition, more common than childhood type 1 diabetes.

**Keratic precipitates (KP)** — clumps of white blood cells deposited on the inner cornea, a
diagnostic sign of inflammation; large clumped ones are called "mutton-fat KP."

**Lens** — the transparent structure that focuses light into the eye; the site of cataract
formation.

**Metamorphopsia** — a visual distortion where straight lines appear curved, caused by retinal
(often macular) problems.

**Optic nerve** — the bundle of fibers carrying signals from retina to brain; where it exits the
eye is called the optic papilla or optic disc.

**Panuveitis** — inflammation across all areas of the eye (anterior, intermediate, and posterior
combined).

**Photopsia** — perceived flashes of light in the field of vision.

**Pupil** — the dark opening in the center of the iris that regulates how much light enters the
eye.

**Retina** — the layer of light-sensing cells at the back of the eye; its functional center is
called the macula.

**Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE)** — the pigmented cell layer between the retina and choroid
that nourishes retinal cells.

**Retinal striae** — concentric surface lines on the retina, appearing after retinal reattachment
(spontaneous or surgical).

**Retinal vasculitis** — inflammation of retinal blood vessels accompanied by evidence of ocular
inflammation and vascular change.

**RETISERT implant** — a surgically implanted, longer-duration time-release steroid implant for
the eye.

**Sclera** — the white outer layer of the eyeball.

**Scotoma** — a partial loss of vision or blind spot within an otherwise normal visual field.

**Self-antigen** — a molecule the body could treat as foreign but normally tolerates.

**"Steroid-sparing" dose** — a low prednisone dose (below roughly 7.5mg) at which most patients
don't experience prednisone's characteristic side effects.

**SUN (Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature)** — a 2004 specialist working group that
established the standard duration- and location-based classification of uveitis still used today.

**Synechiae** — adhesions between adjacent eye structures caused by inflammation (e.g. the iris
sticking to the cornea or lens); a diagnostic sign of uveitis.

**Tear film** — the eye's own three-layer protective fluid coating, which chlorinated pool water
can wash away, temporarily removing a defense against infection.

**Th1 / Th2 cells** — two types of helper T-cell that normally hold each other's activity in
check; Th1 drives pro-inflammatory responses, Th2 drives anti-inflammatory antibody responses.

**TNF (Tumor Necrosis Factor) inhibitor** — a biologic drug that blocks excess TNF-alpha protein
believed to drive inflammation in non-infectious uveitis (e.g. adalimumab/Humira).

**Trabeculectomy** — surgery that lowers eye pressure by removing a piece of the trabecular
meshwork so fluid can drain to a bleb under the eye's surface.

**Uvea** — the pigmented middle layer of the eye (iris, choroid, and ciliary body together),
lying beneath the sclera and cornea; uveitis is inflammation here.

**Vitreous** — the gel-like, fluid-filled space inside the eye that gives it its shape.

**Xen implant/shunt** — a small device implanted to reduce eye pressure, often alongside cataract
surgery.

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `swimming-with-uveitis`
- **URL:** https://livingwithuveitis.com/2022/10/26/avoid-the-splash-swimming-with-uveitis/
- **Author:** Wendy
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/swimming-with-uveitis.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a stable, low-incident year for once, briefly contrasted against a COVID-19 infection, the specific mechanism by which chlorinated pool water raises infection risk for eye patients
- **Anatomy:** tear film, cornea
- **Management options:** swim goggles (with a specific caution about intraocular pressure), rinsing eyes after swimming, and preservative-free drops, a prescription antibacterial drop (Ofloxacin) as an optional precaution for frequent swimmers
- **Important concepts:** a mostly quiet year used as the occasion to research a previously-avoided question, chlorine as an imperfect sanitizer that also strips the eye's own protective tear film
subsections.heading: 2. Avoid the splash: swimming with uveitis

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `treatment-complications`
- **URL:** https://livingwithuveitis.com/home/treatments/complications/
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/treatment-complications.txt`
- **Main subjects:** complications the author has personally encountered, listed by name, how treatment side effects can snowball into their own separate complications
- **Anatomy:** choroid, retina, optic nerve, trabecular meshwork
- **Management options:** cataract surgery, anti-VEGF therapy (e.g. Avastin) for choroidal neovascularization, vitrectomy for epiretinal membrane and complex retinal detachment, glaucoma procedures (SLT, trabeculectomy, aqueous shunt implantation)
- **Important concepts:** complications as often driven by the treatment (steroids) rather than the disease itself, the 10 mmHg SUN Working Group threshold for steroid-induced pressure rise
subsections.heading: 3. COMPLICATIONS

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `coping-when-treatment-fails`
- **URL:** https://livingwithuveitis.com/2020/03/30/coping-when-a-treatment-fails/
- **Author:** Wendy
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/coping-when-treatment-fails.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a specific flare that followed a tapering attempt, told in real time, the emotional structure of treatment failure as a kind of loss, concrete, generalizable reasons a medication can appear not to work
- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** Yutiq implant tapering, followed by a new CellCept/prednisone pulse, then an Ozurdex bridge injection
- **Important concepts:** a steroid-sparing dose as a treatment goal distinct from being off steroids entirely, drug efficacy stated numerically rather than as pass/fail
subsections.heading: 4. Coping when a treatment fails

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `diffusing-the-bomb`
- **URL:** https://livingwithuveitis.com/2022/02/22/diffusing-the-bomb/
- **Author:** Wendy
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/diffusing-the-bomb.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a month-long bleb leak crisis following a trabeculectomy performed six years earlier, the two specific dangers a bleb leak poses (infection and hypotony), a bandage contact lens as an interim fix, and the ordeal of managing it at home
- **Anatomy:** trabecular meshwork, sclera, anterior chamber
- **Management options:** a bandage contact lens plus pressure-reducing and antibiotic drops, autologous blood injection named as the next-step option if drops/lens failed
- **Important concepts:** a bleb leak as a delayed complication of glaucoma surgery performed years earlier, not a new event in isolation, hypotony defined by a specific pressure threshold, distinct from and opposite to the high-pressure complications discussed elsewhere
subsections.heading: 5. Diffusing the bomb

subsections.body:

- **URL:** https://livingwithuveitis.com/2020/10/26/evil-eyes/
- **Author:** Wendy
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/evil-eyes.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a lighter, Halloween-themed exploration of cultural associations between red/glowing eyes and villainy, Traditional Chinese Medicine's liver-eye connection, tried firsthand via acupuncture, the mythological "evil eye" and blue-eye superstition
- **Anatomy:** liver (as framed by Traditional Chinese Medicine, not Western ophthalmology)
- **Management options:** acupuncture, tried for three sessions before the pandemic interrupted
- **Important concepts:** a deliberately playful post exploring symbolism rather than clinical claims, the impossibility of assessing acupuncture's effect on her own posterior uveitis given no subjective flare awareness

- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** anti-inflammatory diet, specific AAO-recommended eye nutrient doses, stress reduction practices, UV-protective sunglasses and swim goggles
- **Important concepts:** food as medicine, reframed as choosing what to include, not just what to cut, a cited correlation between stress/cortisol and active uveitis

subsections.body:

- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** CellCept (mycophenolate) plus a prednisone pulse, with an Ozurdex injection to bridge the taper, melatonin as a sleep aid with cited anti-inflammatory research in uveitis specifically
- **Important concepts:** immunosuppression as a double vulnerability during an infectious pandemic, stockpiling medication and insurance mail-order supply limits as a practical risk-management step

- **Important concepts:** chronic inflammation as a normal protective response that has stopped switching off, self-antigen versus auto-antibody, autoimmune disease occurring in the adaptive immune system versus autoinflammatory disease occurring in the innate immune system

- **URL:** https://livingwithuveitis.com/2024/12/15/prednisone-for-life/
- **Author:** Wendy
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/prednisone-for-life.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a year-long taper attempt, after 13 years on prednisone, ending in the conclusion that a low dose is permanently necessary, fundus photography catching a subtle recurrence her own senses missed entirely

symptoms.raw: A new blind spot appearing suddenly, described concretely as "black spots mixed in with the white snowflakes falling" and a smudge that wouldn't clean off eyeglasses `[¶1]`.
Bilateral activity confirmed on optic photography during the same flare `[¶1]`.
No early-warning symptoms before inflammation and scarring have already occurred, particularly for autoimmune conditions confined to the eye `[¶1]`.
General absence of felt symptoms even during active disease: **"often, I'm oblivious to the whole thing"** `[¶1]`.
A sudden burst sensation in the eye described as comparable to "water breaking" late in pregnancy `[¶1]`.
Severe burning and pulsating pain specifically from the bandage contact lens itself, distinct from the underlying leak `[¶1]`.
Progressive eye dryness during healing, interpreted (correctly, in this case) as a positive sign of the leak closing `[¶1]`.

Red eyes as a visible sign, though not specifically tied to anterior uveitis in her own case: **"It's not uncommon for me to have red eyes (and I don't even have anterior uveitis, which is characterized by inflammation in the visible part of the eye)"** `[¶1]`.
Post-injection bleeding (hemorrhage) at the injection site is described as likely: **"More than likely, your injection site will bleed"** `[¶1]`.
Sensation during injection ranges from a "click" to more sustained pressure, varying by implant `[¶1]`.
New fluid in the retina and a new hemorrhage on fundus photography, discovered on routine imaging rather than felt symptomatically `[¶1]`.
Recurrence of ptosis (drooping eyelid), previously seen after Retisert surgery, noticed again on video calls `[¶1]`.
Easy bruising, dryness, and hair thinning as cumulative side effects across three concurrent immunosuppressive medications `[¶1]`.
A sudden, self-resolving ruptured blood vessel at the site of old Retisert surgical stitches, described as disproportionately destabilizing emotionally despite turning out to be "nothing" `[¶1]`.
Explicitly *no* felt symptoms at the point of recurrence — clear vision, no dryness — with detection made entirely by fundus photography and her doctor's comparative judgment `[¶1]`.
Rapid weight gain and "moon face" at high doses `[¶1]`.
Joint/knee pain severe enough to disrupt sleep at 60mg `[¶1]`.
Chest and neck acne at high doses `[¶1]`.
Feeling persistently warm, described as an under-documented side effect `[¶1]`.
Severe joint pain specifically during tapering from a *low* (10mg) dose, described as unexpectedly worse than tapering had been at higher doses `[¶1]`.
The withdrawal symptom list: fatigue, fever, stiff/tender muscles, lightheadedness, labored breathing, headaches, depression, anxiety `[¶1]`.
Sudden visual glare/smear as the first sign, despite prior corrective surgery `[¶1]`.
Rising intraocular pressure during pregnancy from scar tissue blocking a prior shunt, severe enough to require a trabeculectomy five months after her first son's birth `[¶1]`.
Gray spots in vision as the presenting sign `[¶1]`.
Extreme light sensitivity (photophobia), severe enough to require independent study rather than in-person senior year `[¶1]`.
Flashes of light associated specifically with weightlifting/exertion, preceding formal diagnosis `[¶1]`.
A week of vision loss `[¶1]`.
Light sensitivity severe enough to require altering his home computer setup, and difficulty reading screens during flares `[¶1]`.
No felt symptoms of flare activity in her own experience `[¶1]`.
Initial presenting sign (in early childhood, reported by a parent, not the patient): a visibly red and inflamed eye `[¶1]`.

**Dyschromatopsia** (color vision deficiency), **Metamorphopsia** (straight lines look curved — "caused by problems with the eye's retina, and, in particular, the macula"), **Photopsia** (perceived flashes of light), and **Scotoma** (a blind spot) are each named as visual symptoms a patient might report and have a technical name for `[¶1]`.
Cataracts: clouded, blurred, or dim vision `[¶1]`.
CNV: distorted vision, change in color vision, or painless vision loss `[¶1]`.
High IOP/glaucoma: blurred vision, eye pain, headaches — **"High IOP/glaucoma can have no symptoms, which is why pressure checks are important"** `[¶1]`.
Macular edema: typically painless, first sign is blurred or washed-out vision `[¶1]`.
Papillitis: loss of vision, color vision changes, eye pain `[¶1]`.
Retinal detachment: floaters, sudden flashes of light, or a shadow in the visual field `[¶1]`.
Light sensitivity, blurred vision, floaters, flashes, decreased vision, eye pain, eye redness `[¶1]`.

Diagnostic indicators found on exam rather than reported by the patient: anterior chamber flare, keratic precipitates, synechiae, the HLA-B27 gene marker, macular edema, retinal lesions, and retinal vasculitis `[¶1]`.
Chronic complications named as downstream of the disease itself: cataracts, elevated intraocular pressure, retinal swelling, retinal detachment, and permanent vision loss `[¶1]`.
Permanent loss of a portion of the visual field, described as "a decent portion of the right side of my right eye" `[¶1]`.
Living "in somewhat of a fog," with busy/visually cluttered environments (stores) specifically overwhelming `[¶1]`.

sections.body:
**This page exists to let a reader map uveitis's location-based classification (from `uveitis-overview`) onto actual eye structures** — it opens by framing itself as scaffolding for
understanding, not new clinical content: **"Being familiar with the anatomy of the eye can make it
easier to understand what is happening with uveitis"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The page's organizing move is pairing each structure with the uveitis category that affects it:
**"Ciliary Body: the part of the eye that connects the iris to the choroid... This is the part of
the eye impacted by intermediate uveitis."** **"Choroid: a thin, spongy network of blood vessels...
This is one of the parts of the eye impacted by posterior uveitis (choroiditis)."** **"Iris: the
colored circle at the front of the eye... This is the part of the eye impacted by anterior
uveitis."** The retina is described functionally — **"the layer of cells on the back, inside part
of the eye that converts light into electrical signals sent to the brain"** — with its functional
center named: **"The functional center of the retina is called the macula."** The **uvea** itself
is defined as the umbrella structure: **"the pigmented layer of the eye, lying beneath the sclera
and cornea, and includes the iris, choroid, and ciliary body"** — the anatomic basis for why
"uveitis" covers such different-seeming conditions.

sections.body:
**A deliberate push toward "stability" in early 2020 instead triggered a new flare within weeks of
tapering prednisone off a Yutiq implant — told as it happened, alongside a reframe of what
"treatment failure" actually means clinically.** The trigger moment: **"I noticed a smudge on my
glasses. When I took them off to clean them, the smudge was still there. My heart dropped to my
stomach"** `[¶1]`. She names the deeper frustration directly: **"In my quest for overall health
stability, I had inadvertently destabilized my treatment"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The post pulls in a cited, numeric reframe of drug efficacy rather than treating it as pass/fail:
**"When one looks carefully at individual drugs and different regimens, Dr. Jabs said, any one drug
works about 50 to 70 percent of the time, and any approach works 70 to 85 percent of the time, but
nothing works 100 percent of the time... You can't rigidly stick with a single approach and expect
it to work with everyone. This is where you move out of the science and into the art of
medicine"** (Doran, AAO EyeNet, 2012). It also lists concrete, generalizable reasons a medication
can appear ineffective: **time to "kick in,"** special instructions, drug/food **interactions**,
**dosage**, or simply **"not a match."**
sections.heading: Why "failure" isn't binary

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

She draws an explicit (and explicitly qualified) analogy to grief: **"Receiving a disease diagnosis
is not something you plan on. It can feel almost like the death of your old 'healthy' self...
(Not trying to equate failure of one treatment with the death of a spouse… but feelings are
relatable.)"** The practical resolution: starting CellCept with a prednisone pulse, then **"we
decided to do an Ozurdex injection to allow me to taper down to 10mg of prednisone during this
COVID-19 pandemic"** — buying time to see if CellCept would work on its own, with Humira named as
the next option if not.

sections.body:
**What makes posterior uveitis distinctly maddening for this author, a self-described "scientist
by training," is not the vision loss itself but the impossibility of running any kind of
controlled experiment on her own body — there's no usable feedback loop between what she does and
what her eye does.** Stated directly: **"I'm a scientist by training and an experimenter at heart.
I want to conduct research, form a hypothesis and test my hypothesis"** `[¶1]`, but **"there is no
immediate reaction to anything I've done, or at least no way for me to realize it. By the time
something is amiss, the inflammation has occurred, along with the permanent scaring and possible
or probable vision loss"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

She contrasts uveitis explicitly with autoimmune conditions that do give feedback: **"It's not
like many autoimmune disease where someone eats 'X', digestive issues ensue or when this do 'Y',
they can't get out of bed the next day."** Flares defy her own attempts to find a trigger: **"I've
tried various diets, and restrictions... and different exercise regimes... Flare ups have happened
when I'm stressed (new baby, no sleep) and when I would think least likely (normal routine or a
vacation in Greece)."** A tapering attempt made this concrete: she went off prednisone after 10
years, and **"wasn't off more than a month or two when I had more activity show up on my optos
photos. So, back on again I went."**

sections.body:

article on chronic illness, and: **"I then realized the coincidence of what I had called this
website (living with uveitis). But that is my wish for myself and others: not to just be alive with
uveitis but to be living, in the fullest sense of the word."**

sections.body:
**A bleb — the drainage reservoir created by a trabeculectomy she'd had six years earlier — began
leaking "briskly," triggering roughly a month of escalating intervention (bandage contact lens,
pressure and antibiotic drops, near-hospitalization-level pain) before healing on its own.**
Framed directly at the crisis point: **"my uveitis specialist confirmed that the bleb in my right
eye was leaking 'briskly.' I knew it and hadn't wanted to believe it"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Two specific, named dangers: **"Infection: a leak means there's an opening in the eye. If fluid can
get out, bacteria and other organisms can get in and cause infection such as blebitis,
endophthalmitis, etc."** and **"Hypotony: Normal eye pressure range is 12-22 mmHg. Anything below
this is deemed 'hypotony'"** — she notes patients who've had pressure-reducing surgery **"may live
in the hypotonous range"** without issue, until it causes **"shallow anterior chamber."** Her own
pressure dropped to **"2mmHg during one of the appointments in December,"** far below the normal
range.
sections.heading: What a bleb leak actually risks

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The lens intended to reduce irritation instead caused unexpected pain: **"I woke with severe
burning and pulsating pain in my right eye. I couldn't get it to stop... My husband found me
sobbing in the bathroom sometime around 2:30 AM"** — leading to an ER visit and multiple lens-size
changes before one was tolerated. She's explicit this isn't advice: **"do NOT try this at home"**
after describing attempting to reinsert the lens herself. Autologous blood injection — **"he would
take blood from my arm, and inject it into the bleb to stimulate healing"** — was named as the next
option if the leak didn't resolve on its own, with surgical repair as the last resort; neither was
ultimately needed.
sections.heading: The bandage contact lens ordeal

sections.body:
- A sudden burst sensation in the eye described as comparable to "water breaking" late in

- Severe burning and pulsating pain specifically from the bandage contact lens itself, distinct
  from the underlying leak `[¶1]`.
- Progressive eye dryness during healing, interpreted (correctly, in this case) as a positive sign
  of the leak closing `[¶1]`.

**A deliberately lighter post prompted by her sons noticing that villains in movies have red
eyes** — she has red eyes fairly often from posterior uveitis and goes exploring, half-seriously,

helped."** She reports the experience positively regardless — **"I did enjoy the sessions"** — and

**Lifestyle choices don't replace uveitis treatment, but they're framed as a second lever the
patient can pull toward the same goal: keeping inflammation and immune response under control.**
Stated directly up front: **"Uveitis is a serious condition for which one must seek medical care.
That said, in addition to following a treatment plan, lifestyle choices have an impact on overall
health, not to mention eye health and vision. The goal is to keep inflammation and immune response
under control"** `[¶1]`.

**Written at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic (Washington State, March 2020), this post treats
being immunosuppressed for uveitis as a specific, actionable risk category — not just advice to
"be careful" but a concrete plan across avoidance, medication, diet, sleep, and lifestyle.** Framed
directly: **"Since many uveitis patients are on treatments that work by suppressing the immune
system, diligence when it comes to health and not getting sick is never far from our minds...
This is what I'm doing to protect myself and my family"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The post is candid that her disease didn't wait for a convenient moment: **"Recently, my uveitis
has become active once again and I started CellCept (mycophenalate) and a pulse of prednisone,
both of which suppress my immune system. The timing.. not so great."** An Ozurdex injection was
added specifically **"so that I can start to taper down the prednisone while the CellCept ramps up
(hopefully) to full efficacy."** A practical supply-chain tip: **"my insurance will cover a 90-day
supply online... whereas only a 30-day supply at my local pharmacy is covered"** — worth stockpiling
before shortages.
sections.heading: Medication timing collided with the pandemic

in reducing inflammation associated with uveitis"** — she takes it "an hour before bed every other
night" while on higher-dose prednisone. Diet advice leans on detox-support foods (cruciferous
vegetables, garlic, green tea) and an explicit caution: **"Sugar and refined grains that turn into
sugar can suppress your immune system."** She's candid about the difficulty of the sleep advice
itself given young children and a pandemic: **"Telling someone to get adequate sleep while on
prednisone during a pandemic is a bit like telling them to 'sleep when the baby sleeps.'"**

sections.body:
**In uveitis, a normally protective and self-limiting immune process has become chronic — the
same machinery that fights infection is instead running continuously against the eye (and
potentially other tissue).** Stated directly: **"Uveitis patients may have too much of this immune
system response process going on in the eye (and potentially elsewhere in the body); the
inflammation has become chronic and is no longer an acute response to an injury or invader"**
`[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Inflammation itself is framed as adaptive, not pathological: **"Inflammation in itself is not a
'bad' thing. Inflammation is how the body protects us from infection with foreign organisms... The
immune system response is the first step in the healing process."** The mechanism named: **"Helper
T cells" (Th) are one kind of T lymphocyte. Th cells develop into two types, Th1 and Th2"** — Th1
generates a pro-inflammatory response against intracellular parasites, bacteria, and viruses and
**"suppresses Th2 cells"**; Th2 generates an anti-inflammatory antibody response and **"suppresses
Th1 cells"**. The two subtypes hold each other in check under normal conditions.
sections.heading: The Th1/Th2 balance

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The page draws a specific, load-bearing distinction. **Autoimmune disease**: **"occurs in the
adaptive immune system when a response against a self-antigen(s) involving T cells, B cells, or
auto-antibodies induces injury systemically or against a particular organ or tissue... The immune
response of the body no longer recognizes what is tolerable or not, self or non-self."**
**Autoinflammatory disease**, by contrast: **"typically occurs when there is a genetic mutation in
the innate immune system. In this case there is no pathogen, however the body is reacting as if
one were present."** A quoted passage from Dr. Mark Hyman frames the everyday version of this:
**"Your body is fighting something — an infection, a toxin, an allergen, a food or the stress
response — and somehow it redirects its hostile attack on your joints, your brain, your thyroid,
your gut, your skin, or sometimes your whole body."**
sections.heading: Autoimmune versus autoinflammatory disease

in the form of uveitis. See The Healthy Vision page to read about more holistic steps"** `[¶1]`.

sections.body:
- **Th1 / Th2 cells** — the two helper-T-cell subtypes whose mutual suppression the page describes
  as the normal regulatory mechanism inflammation relies on `[¶1]`.
- **Self-antigen** — "a molecule or organism that acts like an invader (antigen)... but is
  considered tolerable by the body" `[¶1]`.
- **Auto-antibody** — "one that mistakenly targets and reacts with the body's own tissues or
  organs" `[¶1]`.
- **Autoinflammatory disease** — disease driven by an innate-immune-system genetic mutation, with
  no actual pathogen present, distinguished here explicitly from autoimmune disease `[¶1]`.

  redirects its hostile attack on your joints, your brain, your thyroid" — a way of describing

sections.body:
**Without imaging technology, monitoring posterior uveitis would be essentially impossible for a
patient who, as she's said elsewhere, usually can't feel her own flares — this post is a
first-person walkthrough of the specific tests that make that monitoring possible.** Framed
directly: **"One thing about posterior uveitis is that without microscope and imaging technology,
diagnosing and managing the disease would be nearly impossible. It's never lost on me (or my
insurance bill) how these advanced cameras let the outside world in on what is going on in the back
of my eyes"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

**Fundus photography**: a camera-equipped microscope photographing the dilated retina; its value
is explicitly comparative rather than diagnostic-in-the-moment: **"Photographs can be used for
comparisons from visit to visit and year to year which enables doctors to notice even minute
differences... Photographs also leave less room for details lost to memory, interpretation and
error in note-taking."** **Angiography** (IVFA and ICG): dye injected into an arm vein, then
photographed; she notes the practical side effect: **"Both dyes are highly concentrated and will
take about a day to pass through your system (i.e. expect neon urine)."** IVFA is **"not
recommended while pregnant."** **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: light-wave cross-sections of
retinal layers; she compares it favorably to the other two on comfort grounds: **"OCT is
non-invasive, and in my opinion, is much easier on the eyes due to the lack of flash and the fact
that you can blink at any time during the exam."**
sections.heading: The three tests, from the patient's side

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

She credits a concrete facility change with reduced discomfort: **"The Retina Center recently
opened in a new location with new imaging equipment and the difference is night and day in terms of
eye fatigue from having photos taken. The flash is so much less bright."**

sections.body:
**An intravitreal implant injection delivers steroid directly to the eye so the rest of the body
is spared high systemic doses — but "sparing the body" means a real, repeated, invasive procedure
that this post walks through in granular, practical detail from eight rounds of personal
experience.** Framed directly: **"It's a shot right at the target (localized) and allows the rest
of the body to be spared side effects of high doses of steroids"** `[¶1]`, and: **"I've had eight
intravitreal injections. Five in the left eye (Ozurdex and Iluvien) and three in the right (Iluvien,
Ozurdex and, most recently, Yutiq). This is my experience and these are my tips"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

**Ozurdex**: 0.7mg dexamethasone, 6mm × .46mm, injected via 22-gauge syringe, **"projected to
disperse steroids for around six months with a peak concentration at two months,"** FDA-approved
2009. **Iluvien**: .19mg fluocinolone acetonide, 25-gauge syringe, ~36 months, indicated for
diabetic macular edema, approved 2014. **Yutiq**: .18mg fluocinolone acetonide with an initial
.25mg dispersal, 3.5mm, 25-gauge syringe, ~36 months, approved 2018 specifically for **"chronic
non-infectious uveitis affecting the posterior segment of the eye."** Her own comparison of the
physical sensation: **"Ozurdex has a definite 'click.' Yutiq seemed to require more pressure than
Iluvien in my experience."**

metal retractor that holds your eye open"** — a smaller or reshaped speculum, or a pediatric size
for a smaller face, is offered as a concrete fix. During the injection: **"tensing up and increased
blinking will make the speculum more uncomfortable"**; afterward, **"putting an ice pack on the eye
repeatedly for about 20 minutes at a time significantly decreased the bleeding and swelling for
me."** A specific cost figure is given: **"Bills for the injection and the visit run about $13,000
when billed through insurance in my experience."**

sections.body:
**A year of monthly visits and escalating treatment (Cellcept, then Humira, then a series of
Avastin injections) got her inflammation "under control" by her own account, but simultaneously
surfaced a new complication — choroidal neovascularization — showing control of one problem
doesn't mean the absence of new ones.** Stated directly: **"Thus, the good news is, my
inflammation seems to be under control. However, in July my optical coherence topography (OCT)...
showed a bit of fluid in the retina, and there was a new hemorrhage"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Cellcept alone at 1500mg twice daily plus 20mg prednisone **"was still not controlling my
inflammation. So, we introduced Humira"** — a biweekly self-injected biologic blocking TNF-alpha.
She notes a mundane logistical friction of biologic therapy: **"it is mailed in a large styrofoam
box every month (with ice packs to keep it cold), which I feel guilty about throwing away.**"
Cumulative side effects across three simultaneous medications are reported without trying to
isolate which drug caused what: **"I have noticed I am bruising super easily, am more dried out
than before and my hair is thinning a bit... it's hard to isolate what's causing what."**
sections.heading: The medication escalation, and its practical costs

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Imaging (FA, ICGA, another OCT) led to a CNV diagnosis, explained mechanistically: **"the retina may
produce too much vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) which leads to the production of new
blood vessels. The blood vessels grow from the choroid into the retina. However, unlike normal
vessels, these vessels are leaky."** A specific prevalence figure is cited for her exact underlying
diagnosis: **"CNV is commonly associated with Multifocal Choroiditis, which is what I have, and is
found in 32-46% of patients (Neri, Piergiorgi, et al., 2009).**" Treatment is Avastin, **"an
intravitreal injection... [that] works because it blocks VEGF,"** given in a series of three, 4–6
weeks apart.
sections.heading: A new diagnosis: choroidal neovascularization

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Following a 2018 DEXA scan showing "minor osteopenia in my lumbar spine and left hip," a follow-up
scan two years later showed reversal: **"both areas of osteopenia are now in the 'normal/ expected
range for age.' My bone mineral density increased 3% in the lumbar spine and 1.5% in the left hip.
Diet and exercise do work!"**

sections.body:
**Eye makeup doesn't cause or worsen uveitis, but it does carry an ordinary infection risk that
becomes higher-stakes for a patient who's had ocular surgery, because any breach of the eye surface
is now a route to a much more serious complication.** Answered directly: **"can makeup cause
uveitis? No. Uveitis is not an infection and is not caused or exacerbated by wearing eye
makeup"** `[¶1]` — but: **"those of us who've had a trabeculectomy run the risk of blebitis"**
`[¶1]` if an infection reaches the eye through a makeup-hygiene lapse.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Three explicit rules, stated as her own practice: **"1) I don't wear eye makeup to my ophthalmology
appointments. 2) I don't wear makeup after eye surgery until my eyes have healed and I've had
follow-up appointments. 3) I don't wear eye makeup after injections until my course of associated
antibiotic drops is complete."**
sections.heading: When she doesn't wear eye makeup

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Diagnosis changed her buying habits: **"I used to just purchase what was trendy and in cute
packaging. Now I research extensively before buying any of my cosmetics."** Specific ingredients
avoided: **parabens and phthalates** (endocrine disruptors); **TEA and DEA**, which **"break down
into nitrogen, which can form nitrosamines... carcinogenic (may cause cancer), according to the
Environmental Working Group"**; and **talc**, since **"some talc contains carcinogenic asbestos,
although it's required by law to be asbestos-free"** and can itself irritate eyes. She also gives
concrete replacement intervals: **"Throw out mascara every 3 months... Toss eyeliner once a year
and eye shadow at least every two years."**

sections.body:
**Written during the pandemic's worst winter surge, this post captures a specific, concrete
tradeoff many chronically ill parents faced: weighing a child's in-person schooling against the
parent's own immunosuppression risk — alongside a pointed observation about how vaccine
prioritization language treated that risk.** Framed directly: **"At this point, I'm not willing to
risk my vision so that he can spend half his day in a mask. I can't help but feel guilty. Kids need
to socialize right? What is worse – having no social life temporarily or potentially having a blind
parent?"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

She quotes the CDC's own hedged language on immunocompromised risk: **"'Based on what we know at
this time, adults of any age with the following conditions might be at an increased risk for
severe illness... Immunocompromised state... from... use of corticosteroids.'"** Her response
draws a specific contrast: **"'Might be,' as in, somewhere down the list from those with conditions
that 'are' at an increased risk. Among those conditions is smoking, which is a hard pill for me to
swallow... since that's a choice, and uveitis is Not a choice."** In Washington's tiered rollout,
that placed her at **"at least Phase 2... currently listed under 'future phases.'"**

created the 'Complications' page, under Treatments, which includes side effects stemming from

sections.body:
**After 13 years on prednisone and a year spent carefully tapering down to 2mg, the conclusion of
this post — the most recent in the library — is that going fully off the drug isn't achievable for
her: it's a permanent, low-dose baseline rather than a temporary bridge.** Stated directly: **"It
turns out that not taking prednisone is not in the cards for me"** `[¶1]`, after **"having been
completely off for a month."**
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The taper had gone well by subjective measure: **"I don't experience side effects of which I am
aware, even at 5 mg... I began 2024 at 5 mg of prednisone and was down to 2 mg with stable
appointments."** Partway through, she reframes the drug's role in her own mind: **"I began to think
of prednisone as my sort of anti-placebo. Instead of taking a drug that was actually nothing, I
thought I needed a drug, but I didn't. It seemed to be my crutch in tiny pill form."** But she
continued tapering anyway, citing prednisone's known long-term risks named in `prednisone-part-i`
and `prednisone-part-ii`: **"corticosteroids are not known to be something one wants to continue
for long periods of time... especially as a female in her 40's (i.e. bone density risk)."**
sections.heading: The taper, and the psychological reframe along the way

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The recurrence that ended the taper was entirely subclinical from her own perspective: **"My eyes
felt super good this morning; not dry, and my vision seemed clear (for me)... if not for the fundus
photography... and the fact that my doctor knows my eyes so well, it likely would have gone
undetected."** This directly exemplifies the pattern she first named in `diagnosis-story` years
earlier — no reliable subjective warning sign — resolved here specifically by the imaging routine
described in `into-the-eyes-of-the-beholder`.

  detection made entirely by fundus photography and her doctor's comparative judgment `[¶1]`.

sections.body:
**Prednisone is described as simultaneously the drug that reliably controls her uveitis and the
one with the widest, best-documented list of side effects across nearly every body system — this
post is a systematic side-effect survey grounded in over a decade of personal dosing history.**
Framed directly: **"The prednisone did its job; my uveitis was brought to a screeching halt. But I
couldn't stay on the high dosage forever... due to all of the side effects"** `[¶1]`, and: **"I now
am aware of them, long and short term, and what I can do to lessen them"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

**"Prednisone is a synthetic glucosteroid... closely related to and mimics cortisol, which is a
hormone naturally produced by the adrenal gland."** The relevant potency figure is stated
precisely: **"Prednisone... is four to five times as potent as cortisol. Therefore, roughly 5 mg of
prednisone is equivalent to the body's daily output of cortisol."** Mechanistically, corticosteroids
block **"substances that create inflammatory actions called prostaglandins... and white blood
cells... In this way, corticosteroids suppress the immune system."**
sections.heading: Mechanism: mimicking the body's own stress hormone

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

**Adrenocortical insufficiency**: **"since you're taking prednisone, the body senses the level of
steroid is 'high enough' and stops making as much"** — the reason abrupt cessation is dangerous.
**Immunosuppression**: increased susceptibility "from persistent athlete's foot and candida" up to
"serious and potentially fatal infections like chicken pox and measles"; live-virus vaccines are
contraindicated at immunosuppressive doses. **Musculoskeletal**: **"The American College of
Rheumatology... considers patients receiving... greater than 2.5 mg of prednisone daily for three
months or longer to be at risk for bone loss"** — her own 2018 DEXA scan found osteopenia in her
hips, addressed since with increased calcium, vitamin D, and weight training. **Ocular**:
**"posterior subcapsular and nuclear cataracts and/or increased intraocular pressure"** — the same
complications named in `treatment-complications`. **Nervous system**: insomnia, mood swings,
depression — she notes a side effect she says isn't widely documented: **"feeling warm all of the
time, which can also impact mood and sleeping."** **Endocrine**: decreased glucose tolerance,
hyperglycemia, sodium/fluid retention producing "moon face." **Dermatologic**: acne (**"prednisone
acne is real"**) and thinned, more easily bruised skin.

- Rapid weight gain and "moon face" at high doses `[¶1]`.
- Joint/knee pain severe enough to disrupt sleep at 60mg `[¶1]`.
- Chest and neck acne at high doses `[¶1]`.
- Feeling persistently warm, described as an under-documented side effect `[¶1]`.

**Tapering off prednisone is harder, and its risk-benefit calculus during pregnancy and a pandemic
is more nuanced, than "just take less" — this post continues Part I with the practical mechanics
of coming off the drug and two specific situations (pregnancy, COVID-19) where the guidance is
conditional rather than universal.** Framed directly: **"The importance of tapering cannot be
overstated... it's important to wean your body off the supplemented steroid so it does not crash
and leave you with a whole host of painful (and potentially dangerous) withdrawal symptoms"**
`[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

A counterintuitive pattern from her own repeated tapers: **"when I have gone to taper off of
prednisone, from only 10 mg, even when I thought I was tapering slowly, I have had excruciating
joint pain... I felt like I was 80 years old!"** A cited explanation resolved her confusion:
**"'[Withdrawal] Symptoms are milder at high cortisol amounts and intensify when milligrams are
reduced below a certain point. A longer adjustment period is recommended at lower doses'"**
(Adrenal Insufficiency United). Withdrawal symptoms listed include severe fatigue, joint pain,
fever, body aches, and — flagged as rare but serious — **"Adrenal crisis, a rare, possibly fatal
reaction to a lack of steroid hormone in your body."**
sections.heading: Withdrawal gets worse, not better, at lower doses

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

**"I took a low dosage (~10 mg if I recall correctly) during my two pregnancies and while
breastfeeding, and my sons incurred no known side effects"** — stated explicitly as personal
experience rather than general advice: **"I'm not advocating one way or another, this is just my
experience."** She made a specific precautionary choice regardless of the low measured risk: **"I
did make the choice to not donate breast milk to anyone because of my medication."**
sections.heading: Pregnancy and breastfeeding, from direct experience

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

A 139-expert consensus survey on non-infectious uveitis (NIU) treatment during COVID-19 is
summarized with its risk-stratified structure preserved rather than flattened into one rule:
**"Surveyed uveitis experts recommended to not begin systemic corticosteroid or immunosuppression
for NIU treatment in sick patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19, irrespective of risk
group"** — but **"in healthy patients, experts agreed to start oral corticosteroids only in
increased risk patients."** The overarching direction: **"local therapy (regional corticosteroid
injections) should be preferred to systemic treatment in all patients... except in healthy patients
not already on corticosteroids,"** because systemic steroids **"might be harmful, given their
mechanism of action that inhibits the immune responses and affects the pathogen clearance."**

genetic rather than incidental — a fact this post treats as backdrop to her own decade-long,
two-pregnancy experience of managing the disease around childbearing.** Stated directly: **"Women
make up the majority of uveitis patients, young and old (Faia and Drenser, 2017)... In the United
States... non-infectious uveitis is more prevalent (80-90% of cases) (Yeh and Shantha, 2016) and is
most often associated with autoimmunity which occurs far more often in women (Fairweather and Rose,
2007)"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

**X-chromosome inactivation**: **"Since women have two X chromosomes and don't need two copies of
each gene, one of each gene is supposed to be deactivated; when this doesn't happen in an evenly
distributed method, instances of auto-immune disease are more common (Ørstavik, 2017)."**
**Hormonal cycling**: **"Estrogen and progesterone promote the anti-inflammatory response and
therefore suppress pro-inflammatory cytokines"** — and a specific cited study found **"a
significant increase in the incidence of Acute Anterior Uveitis arising late in the menstrual
period,"** postulating that **"the withdrawal of either or both [o]estrogen and progesterone
provokes the onset of inflammation" (Sanghvi, Aziz, & Jones, 2004)**. The same hormonal shift cuts
both ways in pregnancy: rising estrogen/progesterone suppress the Th1 response, which **"can worsen
symptoms in auto-immune diseases associated with Th2 excess (such as lupus) and relieve
auto-immune diseases associated with excess Th1 response"** — and non-infectious uveitis is placed
in the latter, potentially-relieved category (Yeh and Shantha, 2016).
sections.heading: Two proposed mechanisms for female prevalence

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Onset came suddenly at 27: **"the lights were reflecting oddly to me, like there was a glare or a
smear over my lens"** despite prior LASIK; an optometrist's response — **"Is your dad with you?"**
— signaled how serious it was. To get off high-dose prednisone before trying to conceive, her
doctor prescribed steroid-sparing drugs, but **"a major side effect for me was that I was unable to
get pregnant on them."** A 2012 RETISERT implant and new lens allowed weaning off systemic
medication; a naturopath later adjusted her thyroid medication and progesterone, and **"within a
month I was pregnant."** She raises an open question about whether prednisone itself affects
thyroid levels enough to matter, citing Haugen (2009): **"Glucocorticoids such as prednisone can
lower serum Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) levels... however do not induce clinically evident
central hypothyroidism even after prolonged high dose use."**

**A guest perspective from a 19-year-old who shares the site author's own diagnosis of Multifocal
Choroiditis, but with panuveitis rather than posterior-only involvement, diagnosed suddenly during
her final year of high school — and whose response was building the public awareness she
couldn't find for herself.** Framed by the introduction: **"She's got my same diagnosis of
'multi-focal choroiditis,' but with panuveitis, which means that her inflammation is all throughout
her eye"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Onset was sudden and initially dismissed: **"I started to notice gray spots in my vision... My
optometrist... decided to send me to the emergency room"** on suspicion of retinal detachment or
fluid behind the retina — but **"the emergency room sent me back home telling me there was nothing
they could do"** despite extreme light sensitivity a week later. Her own read: **"I went home with
fear and pain. This was when I knew there was something wrong."**
sections.heading: A fast, disorienting diagnosis

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Diagnosis derailed specific life plans: **"I had wanted to attend my high school and go to all the
senior events but I sadly couldn't due to the photophobia... I had also hoped to go to Community
College in the hopes of going to Forensics or Liberal art. This was not possible since my M.C.P was
still out of control."** She names the compounding difficulty directly: **"The Hardest part of all
of this has been accepting that there is a possibility of losing my vision at any time. What has
also been hard is the lack of support and awareness there is for Uveitis."** Her response was to
create an Instagram account (@theflowerintheireyes): **"There is sadly a lack of representation and
awareness about Uveitis. It took me almost a year to find a community... I would not want anyone
else to feel as alone and hopeless as I did."**

**A guest perspective from a 25-year-old web developer with chronic panuveitis in both eyes,
associated with sarcoidosis — notable for naming a specific social friction the site author's own
posts (`what-you-dont-see`) also describe: being young makes an invisible disease even less
believable to other people.** Stated directly: **"As someone who is 25 years old, nobody makes the
assumption that I am suffering from an autoimmune disease which makes it hard to see. Most people
can afford sympathy to older individuals as it's assumed they may have health problems, but younger
individuals are assumed to be in good health"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Onset was gradual and easy to misattribute at first: **"flashes of lights in the corner of my eyes,
associated with weight lifting. Next I lost vision in my eyes for a week when on holiday. Then
finally I arrived in eye casualty in October 2018 to be given an official diagnosis."** Treatment
escalated to **"double eye surgery in my right eye. One surgery for cataracts to replace the lens...
and another at the same time to implant a Xen implant or 'shunt' to reduce the pressure,"**
described as decisive: **"The surgery has saved my life, and restored peace in my mind, as prior to
surgery I was in the most difficult flare up of my life."**

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

As a web developer, he's using his diagnosis to change his own field: **"I am currently on a
journey to make the world wide web a little bit more accessible to those with Uveitis... I have
been thinking of different ways I can help, even if small. To help get a better understanding on
how I can help, or what I should build, I am speaking with others that have Uveitis or visually
impairing conditions."** He also names a specific communication gap with doctors: **"sometimes
doctors can easily end up getting highly technical in their speech and that's when I turn to online
resources where others have put it in simpler terms."**

**This is a guest perspective, not the site author's own words: a first-person interview with a
13-year-old whose anterior uveitis is a direct consequence of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA),
diagnosed at age three — a markedly different course than the author's own adult, idiopathic
onset.** Framed by the introduction: **"Lorelei has anterior uveitis, associated with Juvenile
Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Diagnosed at three after her parents mistook the sign for pink eye: **"my parents had noticed that
my eye was red and inflamed. They took me to the doctor for what they thought was pink eye, but
when the antibiotics for pink eye didn't work... they finally decided on sending me to a child
ophthalmologist."** Early treatment included two surgeries — cataract removal ("with uveitis can
sometimes cause cataracts") and a second surgery to remove resulting scar tissue. Current treatment:
**"I take Humira which is an immunosuppressant which keeps me from having flare-ups... a
bi-weekly injection that I can give myself at home. I also take methotrexate which is a
chemotherapy drug which stops me from having reactions to some of the other medications."** Past
treatment (Remicade) was harder logistically: **"you have to take intravenously so it was really
hard to go to the hospital and miss so much school."**
sections.heading: Diagnosis and treatment, in her own words

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Directly asked whether she can tell when she's flaring, she answers no: **"I've never really been
able to tell when they were happening, my JIA... has only affected my eyes so for me there is
really no tell-tale sign that I'm having a flare-up."** She also states the disease has had
minimal functional impact: **"Honestly I've been really lucky it really doesn't affect my daily
life. I can still play sports and do everything someone without uveitis would."**

sections.body:
**Written the week of a serious personal flare during the George Floyd protests, this post is an
explicit, self-described amateur research effort into what's actually known about race,
socioeconomic disparity, and uveitis outcomes — framed by the author's own acknowledged privilege
in accessing care.** Stated directly: **"I have the privilege of having access to excellent health
care and insurance coverage... that afford me clinic visits, fundus photography, and medication.
Without these things, this flare may have led to a road that I don't let my mind go down"**
`[¶1]`. She's explicit about the post's own limits: **"this is by no means a complete analysis.
It's just me doing some research while my kids are asleep to initiate thought"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Findings are reported with their limitations named alongside them. A 5,106-person self-reported
sample found **"no specific ethnic group predominance, which may be partly due to the small sample
size"** (González et al., 2018) — contrasted with the Pacific Ocular Inflammation Study's higher
incidence in white populations, and a report of **"higher incidence of uveitis in African American
patients with inflammatory bowel disease"**. A Birmingham, Alabama chart review found **"African
Americans are more likely to have panuveitis while Caucasians are more likely to have posterior
uveitis"** (Read et al., 2012). A pediatric study found **"increased severity of poor visual
outcome in non-Hispanic African American children,"** with cause left explicitly open: **"could be
secondary to biologic differences or variance in health-care access"** (Angeles-Han et al., 2015).
sections.heading: What the epidemiological studies actually found

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

International disparity is framed as access-driven, not purely biological: **"blindness due to
uveitis... is reported as 25% in India and other developing countries, whereas... 10% or less in
Europe and the United States"** — attributed partly to infectious causes predominating where care
access is worse (Rao, 2013), while non-infectious/autoimmune causes dominate in developed
countries. A workforce-diversity paper is cited on physician-patient concordance: **"when
physicians and patients share the same race or ethnicity, this improves time spent together,
medication adherence, shared decision-making... Not surprisingly, implicit bias from the physician
is decreased."**

sections.body:
**After a rare stretch of stability — appointments stretching from 6 to 14 weeks apart — she
finally researched a question she'd been avoiding: how risky is regular pool swimming for someone
with uveitis, given that chlorine doesn't just fail to kill everything, it also strips the eye's
own protective tear film.** Framed directly: **"I'd been avoiding researching just how bad pool
water is for folks with eye disease because I didn't really want to know. I finally did some
'googling'"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Two separate facts combine into the real risk: chlorine's imperfect sanitizing (**"Chlorine is a
fairly decent sanitizer, but it doesn't kill everything"**) plus its effect on the eye's own
defenses: **"When your eyes are submerged in chlorinated pool water, the tear film that usually
acts as a defensive shield for your cornea is washed away. This means that your eyes are no longer
protected from dirt or bacteria that are not entirely eliminated by the treated pool water. So,
swimmers can be prone to eye infections"** (Dr. David Williams, OD). The uveitis-specific stakes:
**"Anterior uveitis can be exacerbated by irritation from chlorine or even brought on by parasites,
which would be more common in lakes or other water bodies"** (Saudi J Ophthalmol., 2018).
sections.heading: The actual mechanism

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Four practical steps: wear goggles, rinse off after swimming, use preservative-free drops, and
optionally discuss a prescription antibacterial drop (Ofloxacin) with a doctor for frequent
swimmers. One caution cuts against the obvious "just wear goggles" advice: **"Goggles can cause a
slight increase in interocular pressure, so if you're in the danger zone (i.e. taking drops or
medication to reduce pressure), you probably want to discuss this one with your doctor"** — directly
relevant to a patient like herself with a history of pressure-lowering surgery.

**Being immunosuppressed for uveitis didn't map cleanly onto any public vaccine-eligibility
category, which meant she had to actively hunt for an appointment rather than simply qualify — and
the same mismatch resurfaced getting a third dose, since uveitis is never named on standard
eligibility checklists.** Framed directly: **"people on immunosuppressants due to medical
conditions or disease treatment sat like sitting ducks... I became a 'vaccine chaser' in my town,
calling and asking every clinic and pharmacy to get on extras lists"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The rationale is explicitly immunological, not precautionary: **"Studies have shown that those on
immunosuppressants aren't necessarily making the antibodies when they receive the vaccine. The CDC
says that a large number of hospitalized 'break through' cases are actually immunocompromised
people who didn't make antibodies or enough antibodies."** At the point of service, the mismatch
between her condition and standard eligibility categories surfaced again directly: **"The guy at
the counter asked me if I qualified in a tone that didn't surprise me... Have you had a liver
transplant? Do you have cancer? No, but I take or have taken many of the same medications."**

attend my appointment every 6 weeks at which my doctor gives me an Avastin injection to keep my CNV
at bay"** — i.e., COVID exposure risked disrupting an unrelated, ongoing eye treatment schedule,
not just direct illness.

sections.body:
**A uveitis patient will repeatedly encounter a specific, learnable set of imaging and pressure
tests, and this page exists because doctors use their names assuming familiarity the patient
usually doesn't have** — stated directly: **"it can be overwhelming and confusing when doctors and
technicians start using words and terms that are unfamiliar... This page contains definitions of
tools, tests and terminology that I've come across"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Imaging tests are distinguished from pressure tests. Imaging: the **Amsler Grid** ("detect vision
problems resulting from damage to the macula... or the optic nerve"), **Fluorescein Angiography**
("a fluorescent dye... injected into the bloodstream... highlights the blood vessels in the back of
the eye"; **"Not recommended during pregnancy"**), **Fundus photography** ("high contrast,
high-resolution imaging of the back... interior portion of the eye"), **Indocyanine Green (ICG)
Angiography** ("fluoresces in the infrared spectrum and highlights the choroid layer"), and
**Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)** ("uses light waves to take cross-section pictures of the
retina"). Pressure and field tests: **Pachymetry** (cornea thickness, which **"has the potential to
influence Interocular Pressure"**), **Perimetry** / the **Humphrey** and **Goldmann Visual Field**
tests (mapping blind spots), the **Snellen Eye Chart** (visual acuity), and **Tonometry** (measures
intraocular pressure; **"The normal range for pressure is 12-21 mm Hg"**, and **"the patient should
make an effort to breathe normally during this test as holding breathe can influence the IOP"**).

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Terms tied specifically to uveitis diagnosis: **Anterior Chamber Flare** ("inflammation in the
front of the eye causes the breakdown of vessels in the blood-aqueous barrier... creating cloudiness
(flare) when a light is shone in the eye... a diagnostic indicator of uveitis"), **Keratic
precipitates** ("clumps of white blood cells deposited on the corneal epithelium... start out white
and round and become irregular and faded with age... large yellow KP are formed and termed
mutton-fat KP"), the **HLA-B27 Gene** ("strongly associated with autoimmune diseases including
anterior uveitis"), and **Synechiae** ("adhesions formed between adjacent structures within the
eye usually as a result of inflammation... a diagnostic indicator of uveitis").

sections.body:
**It's not uveitis itself that tends to blind patients — it's the cascade of complications and
treatment side effects that follow it, which "snowball" together.** Stated directly: **"Uveitis, in
itself, isn't necessarily the cause of blindness in patients. As with many other diseases, it's not
the disease itself that creates the most damage, but the complications and ancillary issues, which
are often related and tend to snowball"** `[¶1]`, with a supporting citation: **"Noninfectious
intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis, or panuveitis, particularly persistent disease, is
associated with a substantial risk of ocular complications" (Dick, Andrew D., et al., 2016)**
`[¶1]`. Notably, this list is stated as personal, not exhaustive: **"I've listed the main
complications that I've encountered (except for retinal detachment, fingers crossed)"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Each complication is given a definition, a symptom list, and a treatment: **Cataracts**
("proteins in the eye start to break down and clump together"; treated by lens replacement).
**Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV)** ("growth of new, damaging blood vessels beneath the
retina... these vessels are leaky"; treated with anti-VEGF therapy like Avastin, laser
photocoagulation, or photodynamic therapy) — and its downstream complication, **subretinal
fibrosis** ("scarring... underneath the retina," for which the page states plainly: **"Treatment:
None currently developed"**). **Epiretinal Membrane** (scar tissue on the retina surface; treated
by vitrectomy). **High Intraocular Pressure / "Steroid Induced Glaucoma"** — the page cites a
specific clinical threshold: **"the threshold for considering a rise in interocular pressure due
to corticosteroid to be substantial is 10 mmHg or greater after use of the steroid began"**,
according to the SUN Working Group, with treatments ranging from drops to Selective Laser
Trabeculoplasty to trabeculectomy to shunt implantation. **Macular Edema**, **Papillitis** (loss
of vision "can occur within a few hours of onset"), **Ptosis**, and **Retinal Detachment**
(specifically **exudative** retinal detachment, "the type of detachment most associated with
uveitis and/or ocular surgery").
sections.heading: The complications, symptom and treatment paired

sections.body:
- Cataracts: clouded, blurred, or dim vision `[¶1]`.
- CNV: distorted vision, change in color vision, or painless vision loss `[¶1]`.
- High IOP/glaucoma: blurred vision, eye pain, headaches — **"High IOP/glaucoma can have no
  symptoms, which is why pressure checks are important"** `[¶1]`.
- Macular edema: typically painless, first sign is blurred or washed-out vision `[¶1]`.
- Papillitis: loss of vision, color vision changes, eye pain `[¶1]`.
- Retinal detachment: floaters, sudden flashes of light, or a shadow in the visual field `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV)** and **subretinal fibrosis** as its own late complication
  `[¶1]`.
- **Trabeculectomy** — "a procedure that lowers the pressure in the eye by removing a piece of the
  trabecular meshwork to allow for drainage but still in a controlled manner," with fluid draining
  to a **bleb** (a small reservoir under the eye surface) `[¶1]`.
- **Aqueous Shunt Implantation**, **Ahmed Glaucoma Valve**, **Baerveldt** and **Molteno Glaucoma
  Implant** — device-based alternatives when trabeculectomy alone doesn't lower pressure `[¶1]`.
