sections.body:
**Uveitis treatment is a ladder that runs from minimally invasive eye drops to surgical implants,
and the central decision at every rung is localized (affecting only the eye) versus systemic
(affecting the whole body) — which depends on whether the uveitis is tied to another disease.**
Stated directly: **"If the patient's uveitis is associated with another disease or disorder,
treatment will likely be systemic... whereas if the cause of the uveitis is unknown, localized
treatments... may be an option"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

**Eye drops** — steroid drops (Prednisolone Acetate, Dexamethasone, Loteprednol, Rimexolone) for
inflammation, and dilating drops for the fixed pupils associated with anterior uveitis.
**Immunosuppressants**, taken systemically, don't discriminate between cells: **"the medication
does not differentiate between cells. The patient's entire immune system is suppressed."**
**Corticosteroids** — prednisone is named as usually the first line: **"one of the first
medications prescribed for uveitis, among a myriad of other conditions. It's so commonly prescribed
that side effects may be downplayed or not discussed."** **Antimetabolites** — methotrexate
**"partially inhibits dihydrofolate reductase... within the cells"** and can take **"about three
months before the treatment has an effect."** **T-cell/calcineurin inhibitors** — cyclosporine
("often used in conjunction with Methotrexate... Hair growth is a common side effect") and
tacrolimus. **Biologic agents** — TNF inhibitors like adalimumab (Humira, **FDA-approved for
non-infectious uveitis in 2016**) target excess Tumor Necrosis Factor Alpha Protein.
sections.heading: The drug-class ladder

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Periocular/intravitreal injections deliver corticosteroid directly around or into the eye, a
method described as more common **"before longer-acting intravitreal implants were developed."**
Implants go further — **"injected into the vitreous humor of the eye during an in-office
procedure... release a sustained dosage of the medication over time and eventually dissolve"** —
but the tradeoff is explicit: **"Side effects should not be taken likely and can (and probably
will) include: cataracts and increased eye pressure."** Three specific implants are compared:
**Ozurdex** (0.7mg dexamethasone, up to 6 months), **Yutiq** (.18mg fluocinolone acetonide, up to
36 months), and **Retisert** (0.59mg fluocinolone acetonide, FDA-approved 2005, up to 3 years,
**"contains a higher dosage of medication than the other implants and is larger (about the size of
a grain of rice)"** and is surgically implanted rather than injected.

sections.body:
Not directly addressed as patient-reported symptoms — this page organizes by drug class and
delivery route rather than by presenting complaint. See `treatment-complications` for the

- **Antimetabolite** — "a substance that interferes with the normal metabolic processes within
  cells and prevents them from surviving and/or multiplying by targeting specific enzymes" `[¶1]`.
- **Calcineurin inhibitor** — a medicine that blocks the enzyme calcineurin, which activates
  T-cells `[¶1]`.
- **TNF (Tumor Necrosis Factor) inhibitor** — a biologic that blocks excess TNF-alpha protein

sections.body:
**Uveitis is not a single disease but a group of inflammatory diseases classified by where in the
eye the inflammation sits and how long it lasts — and for at least a third of patients, no cause
is ever found.** The page opens with the clinical definition: **"Inflammation of the uvea; a term
describing a group of inflammatory diseases that produces swelling and destroys eye tissues"**
`[¶1]`, and states plainly that **"Uveitis is the third leading cause of preventable blindness in
the developed world"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Two independent axes of classification are given. By **duration**: acute (sudden, limited),
recurrent (episodes separated by ≥3 months of inactivity), or chronic (relapse within <3 months of
stopping treatment). By **location**: anterior (iris — "the most common type"), intermediate
(often the vitreous, "associated with sarcoidosis and multiple sclerosis"), posterior (choroid
and/or retina, including a rare form called "Birdshot" Retinochoroidopathy), or panuveitis
("Inflammation across all areas of the eye"). This location-based scheme traces to a specific
2004 effort: **"a group of uveitis specialists met in a working group known as Standardization of
Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN)... established terminology and methods for reporting clinical data so
that doctors are all speaking the same language regarding the disease"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: How it's classified

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

Uveitis itself is not contagious, but its *causes* split into infectious (bacteria, parasites,
fungus, viruses — linked to rubella, HIV, herpes, syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease) and
non-infectious (injury, trauma, or autoimmune/systemic inflammatory disease — ankylosing
spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis,
sarcoidosis, Behçet's disease, among others). Critically: **"The cause of non-infectious uveitis
can also be unknown (idiopathic). This is true for at least one-third of the cases of uveitis."**
Two competing mechanistic theories are named without the page picking a winner: a T-cell-mediated
autoimmune process (**"driven by a T-cell mediated autoimmune process and perpetuated by
pro-inflammatory cytokines"**, quoting Yeh & Shantha 2016), versus an auto-inflammatory pathway
where **"there is a genetic mutation in the innate (rather than adaptive) immune system"**.
sections.heading: Causes, and how often none is found

sections.body:
- Light sensitivity, blurred vision, floaters, flashes, decreased vision, eye pain, eye redness
  `[¶1]`.
- Diagnostic indicators found on exam rather than reported by the patient: anterior chamber flare,
  keratic precipitates, synechiae, the HLA-B27 gene marker, macular edema, retinal lesions, and
  retinal vasculitis `[¶1]`.
- Chronic complications named as downstream of the disease itself: cataracts, elevated
  intraocular pressure, retinal swelling, retinal detachment, and permanent vision loss `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Uveitis** — inflammation of the uvea, defined here as a group of diseases rather than one
  condition `[¶1]`.
- **Panuveitis** — inflammation across all areas of the eye, the most extensive of the four
  location-based categories `[¶1]`.
- **Idiopathic** — uveitis with no identifiable cause, stated to account for at least a third of
  cases `[¶1]`.
- **SUN (Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature)** — the 2004 working group whose classification
  scheme this page's location-based categories come from `[¶1]`.

sections.body:
**The vision loss from chronic uveitis is permanent in a way most vision problems aren't, and
almost none of what it actually costs is visible to anyone looking at her.** Framed directly:
**"Even if your eyesight starts to go it can usually be fixed through corrective lenses or surgery.
For me, and those with chronic pan or posterior uveitis, once it goes, it's gone. A blur, a
washout, a 'blind spot,' never to return"** `[¶1]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

The post is structured as a repeated "you don't see" — cataloging what's hidden behind a normal
appearance: **"You would never guess that I've sat through countless dilations, pressure checks,
optic photography, Optical coherence tomography (OCT)... You'd never get close enough to notice the
tiny blue mark from the steroid implant... Or guess that I have two stints to reduce eye pressure
and artificial lenses in both eyes."** It extends to family life — **"you don't know that for a
while I was on immunosuppressants and high doses of steroids that were contra-indicative to
pregnancy; that I thought I would have to choose between vision and having children"** — and to
daily function: **"That busy stores overwhelm my lack of vision. That I'm not as adventurous or
confident as I once was."**
sections.heading: What's actually invisible

sections.body:
`[¶1]`

She names managing the emotional side as a distinct, parallel job to medical treatment: **"I've had
to make the decision that just as I am managing the physical aspects of this disease, I must also
confront the psychological. I've learned to allow myself stages of grief and acceptance. When the
anger comes, I feel it, but I know I can't live there."** The post closes on a reframe away from
victimhood: **"Uveitis is a part of my life but I determine how big of a role it plays to some
degree... I see someone who knows what it is to see."**
sections.heading: The psychological task, named directly

sections.body:
- Permanent loss of a portion of the visual field, described as "a decent portion of the right
  side of my right eye" `[¶1]`.
- Living "in somewhat of a fog," with busy/visually cluttered environments (stores) specifically
  overwhelming `[¶1]`.
